reads: the doctor met his fate while indiscreetly playing with a dangerous pet
text: The official finding on Roylott's death is misadventure with a dangerous pet.

reads: Such are the true facts of the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott
text: The verdict is true as far as it goes, but it leaves out the scheme behind the snake. That may be what the pledge covered: a promise to Helen that kept the real story from the public until her death.
options: The promise was to keep quiet about Roylott's murderous plan
The promise concerned something else in the affair

reads: conveyed her by the morning train to the care of her good aunt at Harrow
text: The aunt at Harrow proves to be the refuge after all. Helen leaves the house alive, as expected.
Watson reports an inquiry into the Doctor's death only. He does not say that Julia's death was reopened, so her open verdict may have stood in public.

reads: come to an entirely erroneous conclusion
text: I took the gipsy theory for a trial balloon. Holmes now says it really was his first conclusion and a wrong scent, abandoned once he saw the house.

reads: to explain the appearance which she had caught a hurried glimpse of by the light of her match
text: Julia was not raving. She struck a light, glimpsed the snake, and described what she saw in the only word she had.

reads: whatever danger threatened an occupant of the room could not come either from the window or the door
text: He says the shutters turned him towards the ventilator, yet he also claimed to have deduced a ventilator before leaving London. Both can stand if he had not yet seen its use, but the tidy order of discovery is told after the event.

reads: the rope was there as a bridge for something passing through the hole and coming to the bed
text: Holmes confirms the reading of the dummy rope as a route from the opening to the pillow, with the clamped bed holding the sleeper at its end.

reads: and that the bed was clamped to the floor
text: The clamp is one of the two facts that set off his snake idea, and the reader did not get it until the talk at the inn. 'You saw all that I did' was true for Watson in the room, but not for me on the page.

reads: a form of poison which could not possibly be discovered by any chemical test
text: The doctors' negative result was the weak evidence it seemed. Poison was there, of a kind they could not find, and the Palmer and Pritchard remark pointed the right way.

reads: a clever and ruthless man who had had an Eastern training
text: The Calcutta years and the Indian correspondent were part of the means all along, and the doctor mattered more than the brawler.

reads: The rapidity with which such a poison would take effect
text: Speed suits the plan, but Julia screamed, unlocked her door, spoke and only slowly sank. Holmes's account does not square her lingering with 'within ten seconds'. The dose or the place of the bite might differ, but he does not say.

reads: It would be a sharp-eyed coroner, indeed, who could distinguish the two little dark punctures
text: This reconciles 'no marks of any violence' with a bite, but it is reasoning and not a finding. No one is said to have looked for punctures on Julia, and Watson does not report any on Roylott.

reads: he must recall the snake before the morning light revealed it to the victim
text: The whistle is a recall made from Roylott's room. That explains why it came after Julia's scream and why it was heard night after night without harm following.

reads: He had trained it, probably by the use of the milk which we saw, to return to him when summoned
text: The saucer is accounted for as the reward in the snake's training. Holmes's own 'probably' marks this as his conjecture.
Snakes have no outer ears and respond little to airborne sounds such as a whistle, sensing vibration through the ground or what they rest on.
exceptions: An animal may learn other cues that accompany a sound, such as movement, vibration or food.

text: As natural history this is doubtful. Snakes barely hear a whistle and milk is not their food. Holmes offers the training only as a surmise, and something other than the sound may have brought it back.

reads: It might or might not bite the occupant, perhaps she might escape every night for a week
text: The method is a matter of chance repeated nightly. That answers why Julia heard the whistle for several nights before she died, and why Helen heard it and took no harm.

reads: I had come to these conclusions before ever I had entered his room.
text: So Roylott's room was confirmation, not discovery. That explains why his question about a cat in the safe came so readily, though the saucer on top may already have been in view.

reads: he had been in the habit of standing on it
text: The chair is answered as I guessed. Its seat showed he stood on it to reach his end of the ventilator.

reads: hastily closing the door of his safe upon its terrible occupant
text: The clang was the safe door, which fits the order of scream, whistle, then metal. 'Obviously' is Holmes's word for an inference, but it covers the sound as the shutter bar could not.

reads: I heard the creature hiss
text: The kettle-like sound was the snake's hiss, and it was the cue for his attack on the rope.
Holmes does not explain tonight's whistle, which came just as he struck the match. It fits Roylott seeing the light through the vent and calling the snake home, but that remains my reading, not his.

reads: With the result of driving it through the ventilator.
text: Watson says this as settled, but he saw nothing at the time. The retreat is inferred from Holmes's upward gaze and from where the snake was found. The inference is sound, though it was not witnessed.

reads: Some of the blows of my cane came home and roused its snakish temper
text: As guessed, the cane drove the snake back and it bit its master. This is Holmes's account of an animal's behaviour, but the order of events bears it out.

reads: I am no doubt indirectly responsible
text: The verdict's 'playing with a dangerous pet' leaves out both the plot and Holmes's cane. He has a part in the death that the public record does not show, which gives another reason why the story stayed private.

reads: I cannot say that it is likely to weigh very heavily upon my conscience
text: He spoke of striking deeper still and said 'perhaps, after all, it is for the best'. Did he mean only to save the sleeper, or did he foresee where a beaten snake would go?
options: He meant only to foil the attempt, and the death was a result he accepts
He thought it likely the snake would reach its master

text: The explanation is complete on the means, but some things stay unanswered: how Roylott found Baker Street; what his 'important business' in town was; whether the income would have survived Helen's death; why Julia lingered when Roylott died in seconds; how a snake could really be whistled home; why the whistle came as the match was struck; what the other 'little changes' were; and why Helen still wore black.

Final picture: facing the loss of £250 a year at each marriage, Roylott made a route from his room to a clamped bed. Standing on his chair, he passed a swamp adder through the vent to go down the dummy rope, and he whistled it back to the safe before morning, night after night, until it bit. Its venom escaped the tests and its punctures escaped notice. Julia died that way, and sham repairs brought Helen to the same bed. Holmes's cane sent the snake back, and it killed Roylott. Helen survived, and the verdict recorded only an accident with a pet.
